security_spec.violation_condition: Kernel writes raw instruction bytes to userspace-accessible memory (e.g., sigreturn trampoline on stack, vDSO code pages, uprobes xol slot) but uses the target process's data endianness instead of the architectural requirement that all RISC-V instructions are always little-endian, causing the bytes to be byte-swapped relative to correct instruction encoding
security_spec.vulnerability_pattern: arch/riscv/**/signal.c or arch/riscv/**/vdso/* or arch/riscv/**/probes/* where __kernel_rt_sigreturn[] or equivalent instruction-byte arrays are written to memory using store instructions that assume data-endianness—check for memcpy() or word stores of instruction immediates without an explicit LE-encode assertion
security_spec.summary: On RISC-V big-endian (BE) systems, instructions remain little-endian regardless of data endianness; the kernel's signal trampoline, vDSO, and code-patching paths must emit LE-encoded instruction bytes into what is otherwise BE data memory, and failure to decouple the two results in corrupted instructions being executed by userspace

findings.finding: copy_to_user() copies the __user_rt_sigreturn trampoline (defined in entry.S:504-507 as 'li a7, __NR_rt_sigreturn; ecall') as raw bytes onto the user stack for nommu configs. The assembler unconditionally emits LE instruction encoding for RISC-V regardless of target data endianness. copy_to_user() performs a raw byte copy with no byte-swap, so the user-visible instructions are always correct LE. Only active under !CONFIG_MMU; MMU configs use the VDSO path (line 438-439) which is pointer-based, not byte-copying.

The VDSO binary (vdso.so) is embedded verbatim via .incbin into kernel .data, then mapped RX into userspace via _install_special_mapping() (vdso.c:142-145). All VDSO .text objects (rt_sigreturn.S, flush_icache.S, getcpu.S, sys_hwprobe.S, vgettimeofday.c, etc.) are compiled by the RISC-V toolchain which always produces LE instruction encoding. No byte-level manipulation occurs between compilation and mapping.

VDSO code pages are installed as VM_READ|VM_EXEC special mapping. The pages come from __vdso_init() (line 63) which uses sym_to_pfn() to reference the kernel-embedded vdso.so binary pages directly — no intermediate byte copy that could introduce endianness artifacts.

memcpy() on line 172 copies raw instruction bytes from arch.ixol (populated by copy_insn() in kernel/events/uprobes.c:1070-1094 reading from the target binary's inode) into the XOL slot page. memcpy() is a byte-copy with no endianness interpretation. The source binary always contains LE instruction encoding. No byte-swap occurs.

The ebreak insertion on line 177 uses '*(uprobe_opcode_t *)dst = __BUG_INSN_32' (0x00100073) — a native-endian u32 store. Currently harmless because RISC-V has no big-endian support, making native-endian == little-endian by definition. If CONFIG_CPU_BIG_ENDIAN were ever enabled on RISC-V, this u32 store would write bytes {0x00,0x10,0x00,0x73} in memory-order, which is NOT the correct LE instruction encoding {0x73,0x00,0x10,0x00}. The same pattern exists in patch_insn_write() → copy_to_kernel_nofault() for kernel text, and in kprobes.c:28-33 which writes __BUG_INSN_32 via patch_text_nosync(). These would all need LE-explicit stores (e.g., put_unaligned_le32() or __BUG_INSN_32_LE) if big-endian support is added.

UPROBE_SWBP_INSN is defined as __BUG_INSN_32 (0x00100073) or __BUG_INSN_16 (0x9002). These are native-endian integer literals. The weak arch_uretprobe_trampoline() in kernel/events/uprobes.c:1743-1749 returns a pointer to a static UPROBE_SWBP_INSN that gets written to the XOL slot via arch_uprobe_copy_ixol(). Under a hypothetical big-endian RISC-V kernel, the u32 literal 0x9002 would be stored as bytes {0x00,0x00,0x90,0x02} instead of the correct c.ebreak LE encoding {0x02,0x90}. Currently compliant since big-endian is not supported on RISC-V.

copy_to_page() on line 433 writes the breakpoint instruction (UPROBE_SWBP_INSN) into the user text page as raw bytes — no endianness conversion. The source value is the native-endian integer relevant to the breakpoint. Currently correct because RISC-V is always LE. copy_to_page() performs memcpy, which is byte-order transparent.

copy_insn() reads instruction bytes from the probed binary's inode via __copy_insn() into arch.insn[]. The source binary always has LE instruction encoding on RISC-V. __copy_insn() uses uprobe_copy_from_page() which calls memcpy() — a raw byte copy. No endianness reinterpretation occurs.

kexec image loader checks endianness compatibility via the RISCV_IMAGE_FLAG_BE header flag (le64_to_cpu() on line 55) and compares against IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_CPU_BIG_ENDIAN). Since CONFIG_CPU_BIG_ENDIAN is not configurable on RISC-V, this is always false and the comparison always rejects BE images. This is correct — a LE kernel cannot kexec a BE image. The instruction bytes within the loaded kernel image are not reinterpreted, just copied as raw data.

arch_prepare_ss_slot() writes __BUG_INSN_32 (0x00100073) to the kprobes single-step slot (kernel memory, not userspace) via patch_text_nosync() which calls copy_to_kernel_nofault(). The UPROBE_XOL_SLOT_BYTES-adjacent ebreak in the nommu sigreturn trampoline at signal.c:39 uses __user_rt_sigreturn[] defined by the assembler in entry.S, which always produces correct LE encoding. These kernel-mode writes are outside the spec scope but share the same pattern as the uprobes user-visible case.
